bib.title: To SMOTE, or not to SMOTE?

question: Does balancing (oversampling) imbalanced binary tabular data improve prediction when strong state-of-the-art classifiers are used as baselines?
hypothesis: Theory on proper metrics and consistent algorithms suggests balancing should not help strong classifiers; weak classifiers may benefit.
contributions: First large scale study of balancing that includes SOTA classifiers (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost).
For proper metrics, balancing helps weak classifiers but not SOTA ones, and unbalanced strong classifiers beat balanced weak ones.
For label metrics with strong classifiers, balancing and threshold optimization give similar quality; threshold optimization is cheaper; random oversampling is as good as SMOTE-like methods.
Identify scenarios where SMOTE-like oversampling helps.
State that AUC is proper under i.i.d. sampling (Theorem 1).

method.summary: Seven classifiers are trained on 73 imbalanced datasets with no balancing, random oversampling, SMOTE, SVM-SMOTE, ADASYN or Polynomfit SMOTE, with a-priori or validation-tuned HPs, scoring proper probability metrics and label metrics at a fixed or tuned threshold.
method.task: imbalanced binary classification on tabular data

datasets.name: 104 datasets of Kovacs 2019 plus 24 imbalanced-learn datasets (KEEL, UCI, PROMISE and others) filtered to 73
datasets.size: 73 datasets (128 candidates; 48 removed as saturated: 19 with Catboost AUC 1, 29 above 0.99; 7 removed for technical reasons)
datasets.split: random stratified 60% train / 20% validation / 20% test, repeated 7 times with different seeds and splits
datasets.source: [21] Kovacs 2019, imbalanced-learn, KEEL, UCI, PROMISE, CoIL 2000
datasets.preprocessing: String features ordinal-encoded; numeric features untouched; majority class 0, minority 1

models.name: SVM (sklearn)
models.architecture: C in {1,10}, loss squared_hinge or hinge; outputs labels only so threshold cannot be optimized

models.name: LightGBM 3.3.1
models.architecture: eta 0.1 N=100, eta 0.025 N=1000, subsample 1 or 0.66

training.objective: each classifier's default (logloss for boosters and MLP)
training.seeds: 7 random seeds with different data splits per {dataset, oversampler, oversampler HPs, classifier, classifier HPs}

other.early_stopping: on the non-augmented validation fold when applicable
other.oversampler_hps: SMOTE and ADASYN kn=3,5,7,9; SVM-SMOTE (kn,mn) in kn 4 or 6, mn 8 or 12; Poly topology star,bus,mesh; desired minority ratios 0.1-0.5 for all (Table 2, Sec 3.6)
other.oversamplers: Random, SMOTE, SVM-SMOTE, ADASYN, Polynomfit SMOTE (imbalanced-learn; Poly from smote-variants)

other.threshold: fixed 0.5 (non-consistent) or optimized on validation fold (consistent)
other.hp_selection: a-priori HPs = best on test data; validation HPs = best on validation fold

metrics.name: AUC
metrics.definition: area under ROC, proper under i.i.d. (Theorem 1)

metrics.name: logloss
metrics.definition: logistic loss, reported also per class

metrics.name: F1
metrics.definition: label metric at fixed 0.5 or optimized threshold

metrics.name: F2, Jaccard, balanced accuracy
metrics.definition: label metrics (full results in repository only)

metrics.name: mean rank
metrics.definition: rank across datasets, lower is better

baselines: classifier with optimized HPs and no balancing
eval.protocol: Mean over datasets and 7 seeds; error bars one SD over seeds; extra checks with normalization, two validation folds and 5-fold CV gave similar results (not shown).

availability.data: datasets from Kovacs 2019, imbalanced-learn, KEEL etc.; full results in the repository

results.quote: Our results support the known utility of balancing for weak classifiers. However, we find that balancing does not improve prediction performance for the strong ones.

Except for MLP and SVM, balancing and threshold optimization give comparable F1.
results.quote: To summarize, except for very weak classifiers (MLP and SVM), balancing the data and optimizing the decision threshold yield comparable prediction performance.

results.claim: With a fixed 0.5 threshold, SMOTE-like methods were not significantly better than random oversampling; with strong classifiers random oversampling is as effective as SMOTE variants.
results.quote: Note, however, that the SMOTE-like methods were not significantly better than the simple random oversampler.

results.claim: Recommendation: for a strong but non-consistent classifier (fixed threshold, cannot tune it), use simple random oversampling.
results.quote: Thus, when using a strong but non-consistent classifier, it is recommended to augment the data using the simple random oversampler.

results.claim: Optimizing the decision threshold is recommended over balancing for compute cost.
results.quote: However, optimizing the decision threshold is recommended because it’s more compute efficient

results.claim: With a-priori (test-tuned) HPs all four SMOTE variants beat the baselines and random oversampling; authors warn this may be HP overfitting.
results.quote: With a-priori HPs, presented in Figure 1(a), all four SMOTE variants achieved considerably better prediction quality than their respective baselines.

limits: Does not explain why balancing helps weak classifiers but not strong ones: 'We leave explaining this disparity between weak and strong classifiers for future work.'
Classifier labelling is inconsistent: LGBM is listed as a SOTA classifier in the abstract and contributions but grouped with the weak classifiers in Sec 4.1/4.2/5.2.
Only binary tabular data; specialised imbalance classifiers and post-processing not evaluated with SOTA models.
Table 3 text layout leaves unclear which threshold column the oversampler rows belong to (only baseline rows show two values).
Additional robustness experiments and F2/Jaccard/balanced accuracy results are only in the repository, not the paper.
Datasets with Catboost AUC above 0.99 were removed, which biases toward harder problems.
Neither drift nor any time split is tested, despite drift being named as a difficulty factor.

terms.definition: A probability metric is proper when it is optimized by a classifier predicting the true class probabilities.
a learning algorithm is consistent in respect to a metric when, given enough training data, the algorithm converges to a solution that optimizes the metric
